extracted.intended_audience: students (MIT) taking or auditing 18.725 Introduction to Algebraic Geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Syllabus/administrative page for MIT course 18.725 (Introduction to Algebraic Geometry) describing logistics, grading, learning advice, references, and a tentative list of topics to be covered or omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor contact
rubrics_metrics.description: How to reach me. The best thing to do is to drop by my office (2-271) or e-mail me (vakil@math.mit.edu). The phone number in my office is 3-2683.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred contact methods are in-person office visits or email; phone number provided for reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office hours and learning method
rubrics_metrics.description: Office hours. To be announced. The course will be small, so I may just have office hours by appointment. In any case, I’m around MIT most days, so please drop by any time | the subject is best picked up by asking questions and talking it through, not by watching someone do it at a blackboard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect office hours possibly by appointment; instructor emphasizes active, interactive learning (ask questions, discuss) over passive lecture-watching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading: problem sets only
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re taking the course for credit, the only component of the grade will be problem sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem sets are the sole graded component. The grader will almost definitely be Ana-Maria Castravet. Problem sets will be roughly weekly, with roughly ten assignments total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to attempt homework even if auditing
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you’re not taking the course for a grade (but simply to learn), you should definitely at least try the homework problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor strongly recommends attempting problem sets regardless of credit status because hands-on practice is crucial for learning the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning strategy: compute and do problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic geometry can be very abstract, and the only real way to learn it is to see how you can actually compute things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on computation and worked problems as the principal way to gain understanding; motivates the central role of problem sets in the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended references (in order of relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: References. We won’t follow any one reference too closely, but it will be useful to refer to the following three (in order of relevance). 1. Mumford’s Red Book of Varieties and Schemes, Lecture Notes in Math Vol. 1358. 2. Shafarevich’s Basic Algebraic Geometry 1: Varieties in Projective Space, 2nd ed. 3. Hartshorne’s Algebraic Geometry Chapter 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hartshorne is a canonical reference but sometimes an intimidating place to learn the material. Other useful references for commutative algebra background: Lang’s Algebra, Eisenbud’s Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry, Matsumura’s Commutative Ring Theory (hard-core reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative topics covered (course scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tentative sampling of topics. Introduction. Algebraic sets. Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz. Noetherian rings and the Hilbert basis theorem. Affine varieties. Projective varieties, and varieties in general. Properties, morphisms, products, etc. Local properties. Dimension. Sheaves. Sheaves and vector bundles. Divisors (on smooth varieties) and invertible sheaves (= line bundles); maps to projective space. Applications of the Riemann-Roch theorem. An example we’ll follow throughout: Complex curves (and in general curves over any algebraically closed field). Other examples: (a) Projective space P^n; P^1 ∪ P^1. (b) Z; finite extensions of Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List is labeled 'tentative sampling'—gives a sense of the principal subjects and examples that will be emphasized during the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics explicitly omitted / course limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics we won’t discuss: quasicoherent sheaves, cohomology, differentials, flatness. I hope to introduce the idea of a scheme to give you some exposure to the concept, but not to use it in any essential way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schemes will be introduced briefly but not used essentially; deeper scheme theory (and related topics) are deferred to the follow-up course taught by Johan de Jong in the spring.
